core: two senses of bias kept distinct: statistical bias (systematic error) and fairness bias (unequal treatment across groups), and the bridge between them
where bias enters the pipeline: biased data collection, unrepresentative samples, biased labels, historical inequalities baked into records
the training-data mirror: models reproduce the patterns in their data, including the biased ones
why it matters: biased models can make unfair decisions at scale
detecting and reducing bias: audit the data, check model behavior across groups, document limitations
supporting: calibration against a reference standard as a remedy for measurement bias
bias can enter at any stage of data processing, not just collection
ongoing monitoring and testing with real-world data after deployment
human biases can be unintentionally replicated by machine learning algorithms

claims.claim: NIST defines bias, also called systematic error, as the difference between a measurement result and its unknown true value; it can often be estimated and reduced by calibration to a reference standard.
AI bias refers to biased results caused by human biases that skew the original training data or the AI algorithm, leading to distorted outputs and potentially harmful outcomes.

Machine learning models absorb the biases of society that are embedded in the data they are trained on; historically biased data collection that reflects societal inequity can result in harm to marginalized groups in settings such as hiring, policing, and credit scoring.
Named sources of bias include sample/selection bias (training data that is not large, representative, or complete enough) and recall bias (labels inconsistently applied during data labeling).
Human biases can be unintentionally replicated by machine learning algorithms, so teams should audit training data and evaluate predictions for bias before putting a model into production.

The fairness principle of responsible AI holds that AI systems should treat everyone fairly and avoid affecting similar groups differently, for example making the same recommendations to people with similar symptoms, financial circumstances, or qualifications.
Bias can enter at any point in data processing, and ongoing monitoring and testing with real-world data can help detect and correct bias after a model is deployed.
Data-driven and AI systems carry risks to individuals, organizations, and society that organizations should manage.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether simply removing sensitive attributes (such as race or gender) from the data eliminates fairness bias.
positions: Some believe that deleting protected attributes from the data makes a model fair.
IBM notes that this naive approach may not work, because removed labels can affect the model's understanding and accuracy, and the pattern can reach the model through other features.
Formal fairness definitions and remedies are owned by the algorithmic-fairness topic.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches that deleting attributes is not a reliable fix; the general practice is to audit the data and compare model behavior across groups, with formal remedies left to the algorithmic-fairness topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the two senses of 'bias' should be taught together or kept apart.
positions: Statistical bias (systematic error) is a property of a measurement or estimation process.
Fairness bias is about a model treating groups of people unequally.
The subject source-map requires the two senses to be kept distinct.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both senses, explicitly keeps them distinct, and presents the bridge: a systematic skew in what gets recorded becomes unequal treatment when a model learns from those records.
